content.text:
I accepted the challenge and saved the revised F4 as `finding.json` (`accepted: true`).

**What still holds:**
- **Large customers:** none of the 51 customers with at least $500k of revenue loses money on any cost basis tested (q198).
- **2021:** it was a one-year dip, not a lasting pattern. Operating margin was 5.36% that year against 14.63%–20.26% in the others (q106).

**What I changed:**
- **Which work looks weakest depends on the cost method.** My claim that every part family covers its cost, and my pick of small-quantity family 6 and family 3 work as weakest, only hold if indirect labour is charged per clocked hour. Charge it per job and family 1 goes negative: it is 52.3% of jobs, with a median job of $902, and swings from +$11.71M to −$444,827 over ten years. Jobs under $1k swing from +$2.60M to between −$1.31M and −$5.21M. Repeat parts losing money rise from 22 to as many as 41 (q185, q197, q208). Jobs of 1–5 pieces stay positive on every basis (q185).
- **New test of which method is right:** neither is. From 2016 to 2025, indirect labour rose 36.7% while invoiced jobs fell 7.3% and clocked hours fell 12.8%. It stayed at 0.75–0.87 of direct labour every year (q232, q234). My reading is that it behaves like a fixed, wage-driven cost, so the records can't say whether low-dollar work makes or loses money.
- **The action changed.** Any minimum or setup charge should be based on job value, not quantity, and looked at for family 1 first. Before that, someone needs to measure what indirect staff actually spend their time on per job.
- **Corrections to my earlier wording:**
  - Outside processing is on job purchase orders after all (q163). It doesn't change any family or band from profit to loss.
  - Purchase orders with no receipt are 29.7%, not the 28.9% I wrote (q230). They are only 4.54% of purchase-order dollars.
  - Part of the rise in cost per clocked hour comes from fewer paid hours being clocked to jobs, not from costs rising (q201).
- **New open item:** 217 jobs created in 2016–2024 were completed but never invoiced, carrying $565,008 of material (q220). That could be cost the analysis misses or revenue that was never billed; it needs its own look.

The `dollars_a_year` figure is $8,295.4 (q234): what the 22 repeat parts lose a year when indirect labour is charged per hour. Charged fully per job it would be $23,174.1. Either way it sizes the problem; repricing or dropping those parts wouldn't recover it, because the indirect cost stays.
